title: VLANs and trunking
summary: Split one switch into several networks, and carry them all over one cable.

steps.title: Virtual LANs
body: A **VLAN** splits one physical switch into separate **broadcast domains**. Ports in VLAN 10 never see frames from VLAN 20, exactly as if they were different switches.
- **Access port**: belongs to one VLAN; the device sends ordinary untagged frames.
- **Trunk port**: carries many VLANs between switches (or to a router/hypervisor). Each frame gets an **802.1Q tag**: 4 extra bytes holding a 12-bit VLAN ID.
- **Native VLAN**: the one VLAN a trunk carries **untagged**.
To get from VLAN 10 to VLAN 20 traffic must go through a **router** (or a layer 3 switch): different VLANs are different subnets.

steps.prompt: Match each term to its meaning.
pairs: One router port with a sub-interface per VLAN

steps.prompt: A VLAN ID is 12 bits; IDs 0 and 4095 are reserved. What does this print?
steps.explain: That limit is why huge cloud networks use VXLAN (24-bit IDs) on top.

steps.prompt: PC1 on port 1 (VLAN 10) and PC2 on port 2 (VLAN 20) of the same switch both have addresses in 10.0.0.0/24. They can't ping each other. Why?
options: Different VLANs are separate broadcast domains: PC1's ARP never reaches PC2
They need different subnets to ping
steps.explain: Same subnet, different VLANs is a misconfiguration: they can't ARP each other and there's no router path either.

steps.prompt: On the wire, is the frame tagged?
items: VLAN 20 frame on a trunk with native VLAN 1
VLAN 10 frame on a trunk with native VLAN 1
Any frame on an access port
Native VLAN frame on a trunk

steps.prompt: Complete the Linux commands that create a VLAN 10 sub-interface on eth0 and give it an address.
code: ip link add link eth0 name eth0.10 type __1__ id __2__
steps.explain: That's exactly how router-on-a-stick works on Linux: one sub-interface per VLAN.

steps.title: VLANs and security
body: VLANs are a core segmentation tool (guest Wi-Fi in its own VLAN, cameras in another), but only if configured carefully:
- **VLAN hopping by switch spoofing**: a port left in "auto trunk" mode lets an attacker negotiate a trunk and reach every VLAN. Set user ports to access mode explicitly.
- **Double tagging**: frames tagged with the native VLAN outside and a victim VLAN inside can leak one way. Don't use the native VLAN for users; tag it or set it to an unused VLAN.
- Inter-VLAN traffic goes through a router, and that's where a **firewall** policy belongs.

steps.prompt: Which change best protects a user port from VLAN hopping?
options: Configure it as a static access port in the user VLAN and disable trunk negotiation
Put all users in the native VLAN
steps.explain: Never let an end-user port negotiate a trunk.

steps.title: A VLAN-aware switch
prompt: Write a class `VlanSwitch` that floods frames (no MAC learning):
- `void Access(int port, int vlan)` and `void Trunk(int port, List<int> allowed, int native)` configure ports.
- `List<(int Port, int? Tag)> Flood(int inPort, int? tag)` returns, in port order, where a broadcast arriving on `inPort` goes and with which tag.
Rules: on an access port the frame's VLAN is the port's (a tagged frame arriving there is dropped: return empty). On a trunk, an untagged frame belongs to the native VLAN,
and a VLAN not in `allowed` is dropped. It leaves through every other port in that VLAN: access ports untagged (`null`), trunks tagged, except the trunk's native VLAN which is untagged.
solution: private readonly Dictionary<int, int> access = new();
private readonly Dictionary<int, (HashSet<int> Allowed, int Native)> trunks = new();
public void Access(int port, int vlan) => access[port] = vlan;
public void Trunk(int port, List<int> allowed, int native) => trunks[port] = (new HashSet<int>(allowed), native);
public List<(int Port, int? Tag)> Flood(int inPort, int? tag)
if (access.TryGetValue(inPort, out int av)) { if (tag != null) return new(); vlan = av; }
else if (trunks.TryGetValue(inPort, out var t)) { vlan = tag ?? t.Native; if (!t.Allowed.Contains(vlan)) return new(); }
var result = new List<(int Port, int? Tag)>();
if (access.TryGetValue(p, out int v)) { if (v == vlan) result.Add((p, null)); }
if (tr.Allowed.Contains(vlan)) result.Add((p, vlan == tr.Native ? null : vlan));
template: Dojo.Eq("from access 10", new List<(int Port, int? Tag)> { (2, null), (4, 10), (5, null) }, dojoV.Flood(1, null));
Dojo.Eq("from access 20", new List<(int Port, int? Tag)> { (4, 20) }, dojoV.Flood(3, null));
Dojo.Eq("tagged 10 on trunk 4", new List<(int Port, int? Tag)> { (1, null), (2, null), (5, null) }, dojoV.Flood(4, 10));
Dojo.Eq("untagged on trunk 5 is native 10", new List<(int Port, int? Tag)> { (1, null), (2, null), (4, 10) }, dojoV.Flood(5, null));
Dojo.Eq("native 1 not allowed", new List<(int Port, int? Tag)>(), dojoV.Flood(4, null));
Dojo.Eq("tagged frame on access port dropped", new List<(int Port, int? Tag)>(), dojoV.Flood(1, 10));
hints: Work out the frame's VLAN first; return an empty list when it must be dropped.
Then loop over all configured ports in order, skipping `inPort`.
